tossups.text: One thinker who used this language wrote the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus and later introduced the idea of "private languages." Another thinker used this language to argue that a thesis and its opposing antithesis from a new synthesis in a namesake dialectic, illustrated in the book The Phenomenology of Spirit. A work originally in this language calls for workers to take control of the means of production, and was co-written by the author of Das Kapital. For 10 points, name this language used by G. W. F. Hegel and Karl Marx.

The lowest part of this region is the D double prime layer, and the Lehmann discontinuity, located in the low-velocity zone of this region, is an abrupt increase in P and S waves underneath continents. Movement of tectonic plates is caused by convection currents in this layer, and the upper layers of it are the asthenosphere and the lithosphere. For 10 points, name this largest layer of Earth between the core and crust.

In a novel with this language in its title, Bear Bavinsky burns most of his paintings. A "teacher" of this language titles that 2018 novel by Tom Rachman. The author says "good luck" in a "cracked" attempt at this language in a Richard Hugo poetry collection that reflects on the author's military experiences. Jhumpa Lahiri originally wrote "The Boundary" in this language. A poetic form that originated in this non-English language was used by another author to write the lines "One luminary clock against the sky / Proclaimed the time was neither wrong nor right" and "I have been one acquainted with the night." Locals speaking this language populate the predominant settings of Roderick Hudson, A Farewell to Arms, and Catch-22. For 10 points, name this native language spoken by the title character of Mario Puzo's The Godfather.

A scoundrel created by this author writes "Souvenirs of a Soldier in Africa" in La Vie Francaise with the help of Charles Forestier's wife. A character created by this author is stabbed in the neck by a prostitute named Rachel with a dessert knife. Other characters created by this author of "Mademoiselle Fifi" attempt to travel to Le Havre [luh A-vruh], but are held up until the plump title character sleeps with a Prussian officer. This author wrote a story in which Mathilde [ma-TEELD] and her husband borrow a lot of money to replace the titular piece of jewelry, which turns out to be fake. For 10 points, name this French author of "Ball of Fat" and "The Necklace."

This author probably translated a poem that begins "from the great above she opened her ear to the great below". This author's poems are largely addressed to buildings such as "House of the subterranean waters" and "house of the numerous perfect oxen", one of which is referred to as a "pure place cleansed with the potash plant" and another as a "great lion of the wildlands". In the only known depiction of this author, the hairdresser Illum Palilis and the scribe Sagada are also shown. Two of this author's works translate as "The Great-Hearted Mistress" and "Goddess of the Fearsome Powers" from the Akkadian, and this author or someone influenced by this author translated the "Descent of Inanna" from the Sumerian. For 10 points, name this high priestess of Inanna and daughter of Sargon of Akkad, the first named female author.

This character watches a lion and a unicorn fight over a crown, and although her cat Dinah will not talk to her, the Tiger Lily and the other flowers will. She shrinks after drinking a potion labeled "Drink Me," and attends a tea party with a sleepy Dormouse, a March Hare, and a Mad Hatter. For 10 points, name this girl from Through the Looking Glass, a Lewis Carroll character that also went on Adventures in Wonderland.

At the end of this play, the chorus repeats the adage that "no man should be considered fortunate until he is dead." In this play, the title character confronts the blind prophet Tiresias [Ty-ree-see-us] and Jocasta hangs herself. In this play, Thebes is cursed with a plague because the murderer of King Laius was never brought to justice. The title character blinds himself when he discovers that he has killed his father and married his mother. For 10 points, name this ancient Greek tragedy written by Sophocles.

This author wrote a novel whose protagonist is in love with Ann Rush and works at a nameless penal colony inhabited by prisoners such as Quinn and Thomas Ewers. In addition to that novel about Phelim Halloran, he wrote a novel about an unconventional priest named Father Maitland. Historical events which formed the basis for works by this author include the 1918 peace talks in the Forest of Compiègne and the Battle of Antietam. He won the Miles Franklin Award two years in a row for Bring Larks and Heroes and Three Cheers for the Paraclete. He also wrote a novel in which Mort and Jackie Smolders are caught up in the violent rage of the title character, an Aboriginal man who goes on a killing spree. He won the Booker Prize for a historical novel including characters like Amon Goeth. For 10 points, name this author of The Chant of Jimmie Blacksmith and Schindler's Ark.

In one study, this writer described how no lines of less than ten syllables or lines with extrametrical syllables mid-line were used in the prosody Paradise Lost; that work would later influence his use of Neo-Miltonic syllabics in "Poor Poll". This poet described how "The daily thoughts of labour and sorrow slumber/At the sight of the beauty that greets them, for the charm they have broken" in one poem. While living in Yattendon, this man translated Joachim Neander's "All my Hope on God is Founded". This poet arranged the posthumous publication of the works of Gerard Manley Hopkins. For 10 points, identify this Poet Laureate of "London Snow" who published The Testament of Beauty aged 85.

This man discussed his new general philosophy of "science in general, of religion, work, management" and called it a Weltanschauung in his 1971 work The Further Reaches of Human Nature, while he noted that "a musician must make music, a artist must paint... if he is to be ultimately at peace with himself" in his work titled Motivation and Personality. After meeting Kurt Goldstein, he developed his most famous notion in Towards a Psychology of Being, stating that after physiological requirements are met, one must be emotionally fulfilled before reaching his or her full potential. Furthering the notion of "self-actualization," this is, For 10 points, which American psychologist best remembered for his "hierarchy of needs"?

This author is the subject of the leftmost of the three columns on each page of Bottom's Dream, a Finnegans Wake-like novel written by a translator of this author, Arno Schmidt. Walter Benjamin ["VALL-tuh BEN-yah-meen"] described a story by this author as an "X-ray of a detective story"; that story's convalescent narrator is identified with the flâneur in the essay "A Painter of Modern Life." Jules Verne wrote The Sphinx of the Ice Fields as a sequel to a novel by this author that ends abruptly in Antarctica. This American author inspired Stéphane Mallarmé and other Symbolists poets who read him in Charles Baudelaire's translations. This author of "The Man of the Crowd" and Arthur Gordon Pym used Paris as the setting for his tales of ratiocination. For 10 points, name this author who wrote about C. Auguste Dupin ["see oh-GOOST doo-PAN"] in "Murders on the Rue Morgue."

Cancers in cells that secrete this substance can cause pseudomyxoma ("pseudo-mix-oma") peritonei, a condition characterized by ascites ("ass-SITE-eez") of this substance. This substance is contained in the "finger holes" of signet ring cells. Darkly-staining serous cells are contrasted with "empty"-looking cells that release this substance. A heavily-glycosylated protein component of this substance containing serine and threonine tandem repeats has a bottlebrush structure that enables its pH-tunable hydration. This substance's shrinkage upon acidification leads to colonization by S. aureus and P. aeruginosa in people with delta-F508 mutations. Goblet cells secrete this substance to replenish the layer of it in the respiratory and GI tracts. For 10 points, name this lubricant substance that is abnormally viscous in patients with cystic fibrosis.

Under Constantine I, attempting to do this to a person without proving them "a murderer, a preparer of poison, or a disturber of tombs" could result in being deported to an island. Cherokee could perform this action by placing a deerskin outside of their dwelling and placing a person's belongings on it. A "Velvet" one of these actions was opposed by Vaclav Havel and split Czechoslovakia into the Czech Republic and Slovakia. "The Great Matter" was the term Henry VIII use to refer to this action, which he managed to perform with Catherine of Aragon. For 10 points, name this action, historically involving remission of a dowry, by which a couple's marriage ends.

A dimensionless quantity named after this force can be calculated using the Haaland equation or the Darcy-Weisbach equation. A quantity named after this force is plotted against the Hersey number on a Stribeck curve. This non-electrostatic force is independent of velocity by Coulomb's law, and is independent of apparent surface area by the second of Amontons' laws. Electricity is produced by this force in the triboelectric effect. The static form of this force equals the normal force times its namesake coefficient, denoted mu ("moo"). Lubricants reduce the effect of this force. For 10 points, name this force that resists objects sliding past each other.

This adjective describes a phenomenon that causes galaxies to move towards the Hydra-Centaurus Supercluster. Axions may be a "cold" substance described with this adjective, while neutrinos may be the "hot" form of that substance. This word also describes a period before the first neutral matter was formed. An agent described by this word is proposed as the cause of the accelerating expansion of the universe, and a substance described by this word is thought to be made up of weakly interacting massive particles. For 10 points, name this adjective that describes matter and energy undetectable by electromagnetic radiation and thought to compose most of the universe.

In one lay, this figure worries that the ground trembling at the approach of a horseman indicates her "brother's slayer" has arrived. A god opines the nine nights he will have to wait to meet this figure at Barri, and is possibly depicted with her on gold foil plaques called gullgubber. This figure instructs a messenger to take a "frost-cup" of mead after she is told she will sit "on the eagle's hill," marry a three-headed giant, and be cursed with runes for "longing and madness and lust." "All the sea and sky" are described as gleaming from the glittering arms of this figure, who refuses offers of Draupnir or eleven golden apples after she is glimpsed from Odin's high seat. A god is doomed to fight with only an antler at Ragnarok after giving away his sword so that Skirnir will assist in wooing this figure. For 10 points, name this giantess who marries Freyr.

Volcanic eruptions on this structure may create pillow lava if their magma quickly cools. Various oozes and manganese nodules are among the features found in this place. This place subducts into the mantle, and giant tube worms live near its hydrothermal vents. Divergent plate boundaries may cause this structure's "spreading" at mid-ocean ridges. For 10 points, name this structure located at the bottom of the ocean.
acceptableAnswers: ocean floor before "bottom of the ocean"

tossups.text: This man created a set of laws known as the Yassa Code. This man's struggle for power against Jamukha led him to fight and defeat the Naimans, whom he later incorporated into his rule. This man's Jochi participated in his brutal conquest of the Khwarezmian Empire, and he was succeeded by his other son Ogedei. Conqueror of the Chinese Jin and Xia empires, for 10 points, name this grandfather of Kublai, a ruler who conquered the largest land empire in history after unifying the Mongols.

Replacing a vector quantity in this law with the gradient of a scalar gives Poisson's equation. One formulation of this law gives rho-free in terms of the divergence of the D-field. For a charged cylinder, applying this law involves constructing a larger cylinder. Using this law, one can derive the formula "sigma over epsilon-nought" for an infinite sheet of charge by constructing a "pillbox." In its integral formulation, this law involves calculating the charge enclosed by an imaginary surface and the electric flux through that surface. For 10 points, give this first of the Maxwell equations, named for the German namesake of the normal distribution.

An ion of this functional group nucleophilically displaces a chloride ion in the first step of the Banert cascade. In a classic synthesis, sulfinic acid and one of these functional groups are produced from a diazonium salt and a sulfonamide. Alkyl versions of this functional group are produced from aliphatic alcohols in a variant of the Mitsunobu reaction. Tri-phenyl-phosphine may be used as the reducing agent to convert these functional groups into amines. Acyl versions of this functional group are heated to yield an isocyanate in the Curtius rearrangement. These compounds are also joined with alkynes via cycloaddition in a click chemistry reaction named for Huisgen. The simplest example of these compounds is the dominant propellant in airbags. For 10 points, name this functional group containing three nitrogen atoms linked by two double bonds.

parts.text: Name this early American pamphleteer who attempted to inspire rebelling colonists during the American Revolution with his pamphlet series "The American Crisis."
Thomas Paine argued that it was absurd for a continent to be ruled by an island in this pamphlet, which advocated for the separation of the American colonies from Britain.
Common Sense was published in this year, the same year that the United States declared independence.

bonuses.leadin: This author justified revolution in Rights of Man, and declared "these are the times that try men's souls." For 10 points each,

parts.text: Name these biological structures, which are the primary site of photosynthesis. Their distinctive color is a result of their chlorophyll content.
Leaves are found on these organisms, which make up a phylogenetic kingdom. Botany is the scientific study of these organisms.

While most plants produce energy through photosynthesis, a few do not, including the pure white "ghost plant", which is a parasite that gets energy from these organisms. These organisms form symbiotic relationships with plants in mycorrhizae (MY-coh-RYE-zae).

bonuses.leadin: These structures contain palisade cells and pores called stomata. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this sort of book produced by authors from the Franco-Belgian bande dessinée ("bond DEH-see-nay") tradition. Persepolis is a French-language book in this form.

A French graphic memoir by David B. explores the author's brother's struggles with this condition. In a Russian novel, Smerdyakov conceals the murder of his employer by pretending to be suffering from this condition.

Peter Sís's graphic memoir The Wall and a comic book series by Vittorio Giardino both are set in this city. In a novel primarily set in this non-French city, a dissident couple names their dog Karenin after one of them reads Anna Karenina.

bonuses.leadin: Marguerite Abouet ("ab-WAY") wrote vignettes about growing up in Côte d'Ivoire in Aya of Yopougon, which is a book of this type. For 10 points each:

parts.text: It was written by this dash-loving Amherst-dwelling recluse, whose other poems include "I'm Nobody! Who are you?", "I Heard a Fly Buzz When I Died", and "Because I could not stop for Death".

It lent its title to Wild Nights!, a collection of stories about the last days of Dickinson and other authors by this incredibly prolific female author of "Where Are You Going, Where Have You Been?", them, and We Were the Mulvaneys.

It speaks of being "done with" both "the chart" and one of these objects. John Donne spends the last three stanzas of "A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning" comparing himself and his wife to one of them.

bonuses.leadin: Answer the following about the poem "Wild Nights! Wild Nights!", for 10 points each.

parts.text: Identify this queen of Lydia, possibly best-known for wearing the lionskin cloak of a certain hero during that hero's year of servitude under her.

This hero's accidental murder of Iphitus led to the aforementioned punishment, during which he fathered a son named Agelaus or Lamos with Omphale. His other adventures included the twelve labors he performed for Eurystheus.
During Heracles's time in Lydia, these rascally forest demons stole his weapons. In retribution, he tied them to a pole, heads downward. In another story, Zeus transformed them all into monkeys.

bonuses.leadin: This daughter of the river god Iardanus was married to the mountain god Tmolus, and when Tmolus was gored to death by a bull she ruled his kingdom on her own. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this Norse guardian deity. They can see into all nine realms and can hear grass grow, so they can blow his Gjallarhorn when Ragnarök begins.
Heimdall guards this rainbow bridge from the jötnar. This bridge connects Asgard to Midgard.
Heimdall fought this other deity over the necklace Brisingamen while they were both transformed into seals. Heimdall is prophesied to kill, and be killed, by this Norse trickster god.

bonuses.leadin: This deity was born from nine fire demons of Muspellheim ["mus-pehl-hyme"]. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this man, who cheats death by binding Thanatos in his own chains. Eventually, he is condemned to push a boulder up a hill forever in Tartarus.
Sisyphus legendarily founded this city, which hosted non-Olympic "Games" named for the isthmus connecting the Peloponnese to the rest of Greece.

In some traditions, Sisyphus was the father of this man because he assaulted Anticlea as revenge for Autolycus stealing his cattle. This "man of many turns" is first recognized in his home kingdom by the wet nurse Eurycleia.

bonuses.leadin: This man assaults his niece Tyro to take revenge on his brother Salmoneus. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this civil rights leader who worked with Chandler Owen to publish the slogan "Garvey Must Go" in his magazine The Messenger.
Randolph originally orchestrated the March on Washington as a campaign for this cause, enacted by Truman's Executive Order 9981.
The LCCR was a cooperative endeavor between Randolph and Roy Wilkins, the executive secretary of this organization founded by leaders like W.E.B. DuBois and Ida B. Wells.

bonuses.leadin: Following a major victory, this man stated "At the banquet table of nature, there are no reserved seats. You get what you can take, and you keep what you can hold." For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this poorly-attended event that occurs at the end of a 1949 play. Only Happy remains optimistic during it, saying "I'm going to beat this racket!"
acceptableAnswers: the funeral at the end of Death of a Salesman
the last scene of Death of a Salesman

parts.text: As the title would suggest, Willy Loman dies in this playwright's Death of a Salesman. He allegorized the McCarthy-era witch hunts in The Crucible.

This son of Willy Loman and brother of Happy Loman sets much of the plot of Death of a Salesman in motion by returning home from his travels. He was a promising athlete until he caught his father having an affair.

bonuses.leadin: This event ends with a woman sobbing through the words "we're free" as flute music plays. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this psychologist whose The Righteous Mind argues that partisan divisions in America are enhanced by confirmation bias and motivated reasoning, such as that omnipresent in liberal academia. He recently argued for viewpoint diversity with Greg Lukianoff in "The Coddling of the American Mind."

Though he's a psychologist, Haidt is also a professor of leadership at NYU's Stern school, which is this kind of professional school. Mainstays of their coursework include finance and management classes.

This engineer's Principles of Scientific Management were widely taught in business schools in the early 20th century; his ideas were expanded into the field of industrial psychology by Hugo Munsterberg.

bonuses.leadin: This psychologist's "The Emotional Dog and its Rational Tail" outlines his social intuitionist theories. For 10 points each:

parts.text: This poet wrote a poem titled "V" in which the speaker visits a cemetery that is covered with graffiti left by Leeds United fans saying "CUNT, PISS, SHIT and (mostly) FUCK!"
This author's debut novel V. concerns the "schemil and human yo-yo" Benny Profane and his association with the Whole Sick Crew.
This graphic novelist and comic book writer wrote about a Guy Fawkes inspired anarchist activist in V for Vendetta.

bonuses.leadin: Answer some questions about the letter 'v' in literature, for 10 points each.

parts.text: Name this technique used in mass spectroscopy in which an applied potential causes the formation of a fine aerosol containing the sample.
ESI and MALDI are considered this sort of ionization technique which produces relatively few fragment ions, making these methods more suitable for the analysis of large biomolecules.
This method of ionization involves mixing the analyte into a liquid matrix material, then hitting it with a high-energy beam of neutral atoms such as xenon to generate molecular ions.

bonuses.leadin: In this technique, a droplet undergoes Coulomb fission once it reaches its Rayleigh limit, for 10 points each:

parts.text: This man was head of the Confederate Army of the Tennessee for the first half of 1864, until he was replaced by John Bell Hood. He fought William Tecumseh Sherman at Kenesaw Mountain and New Hope Church.
Johnston was replaced after failing to adequately defend this important railroad city in Georgia. After taking this city, Sherman began his March to the Sea, which ended at Savannah.
Earlier, Joseph Johnston failed to break this man's successful siege of Vicksburg. In 1862, this man beat Albert Sidney Johnston and P.G.T. Beauregard at the Battle of Shiloh.

bonuses.leadin: Answer some questions about the collapse of the Confederacy in the West, for 10 points each.

parts.text: Name these diagrams, sometimes colloquially called family trees, which are used to trace genetic disorders in families. In these diagrams, circles represent females and boxes represent males.
A pair of unaffected people have several children. None of the daughters have the disease, but half of the sons do. What's the most likely mode of inheritance for this condition?
A consanguineous marriage is indicated on a pedigree in this way.
acceptableAnswers: any answer mentioning a double line

bonuses.leadin: These diagrams can use diamonds to indicate persons of unknown gender. For 10 points each:

parts.text: The LMAN brain area and FOXP2 gene help birds such as the zebra finch acquire this critical period-governed faculty which is aided by an organ called the syrinx.
This foot-long Jurassic-era fossil is now classified as a bird. Though it was found near fossilized feathers and has long wingbones, we cannot know if it flew or glided.
Many biologists think that this process undergone by the skeletons of birds, in which cavities open up within the bones, helps them fly. In human skulls this process created the sinuses.

bonuses.leadin: Answer these questions about the evolution of birds, for 10 points each.

parts.text: Name this dual-wielding activity, whose pre-game rituals saw participants "go to the water" with a shaman before receiving 300 ritualistic cuts meant to secure victory. This activity, which the Cherokee called anetsa, was used to settle minor disputes in order to dissuade war.
The Iroquois legend of the Creator's Game more closely resembles this other sport derived from stickball. Ireland withdrew from this sport's 2022 World Games to allow the Haudenoasunee to compete.
In one tale, this culture hero introduces lacrosse to the Wabanaki after defeating the wizard Winpe. In another tale, this figure defeats a giant frog that consumed the world's water supply.

bonuses.leadin: In the Cherokee version of the "Creator's Game" tale, bat and flying squirrel receive their aerial attributes during this "great ballgame" between the animals and the birds. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Identify this American chemist whose namesake "dot diagrams" show how valence electrons form bonds or exist as lone pairs.
Lewis defined these substances as acceptors of electron pairs. They have a low pH in solution.
A substance that fits the Lewis acid definition but not other popular definitions is the trifluoride of this group 13 metalloid.

bonuses.leadin: He was the first chemist to isolate a pure sample of heavy water. For 10 points each,

parts.text: Give this name of two emperors of Brazil. While the second ruler of this name was away in Europe, his daughter Isabel signed the Golden Law in 1888.

The aforementioned Golden Law officially made Brazil the last country in the Western hemisphere to abolish this practice. As part of this practice, people from Africa were purchased by European colonists and brought to Brazil through ships in the Middle Passage.
acceptableAnswers: accept descriptive answers like selling slaves

parts.text: Slaves in colonial Brazil were often brought to plantations to cultivate this foodstuff, which was also harvested in colonies like Haiti. This foodstuff was called "white gold" and often shipped overseas in the form of molasses.

bonuses.leadin: The Ipiranga Brook commemorates the location where a ruler with this name gave a "Cry" declaring Brazilian independence. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this force that opposes the direction of motion.
Friction depends on the magnitude of this force between an object and a surface. For a block on an incline, it equals mg times the cosine of the angle of the incline.
The French scientist Guillaume Amontons discovered the following two laws of friction: the frictional force depends on the normal force, and the frictional force does not depend on this quantity.

bonuses.leadin: In the triboelectric effect electric charge is transferred during this process. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this statistical test named for a Japanese mathematician that is used to distinguish between neutral evolution or selection.
An example of non-neutral evolution is this disorder, characterized by red blood cells taking on an abnormal shape. Carriers of this disease are notably resistant to malaria.

A high enough Tajima's D may indicate that this process is occuring, in which the two extremes of a continuous trait are selected for. The opposite of this type of selection is called balancing selection.

bonuses.leadin: This statistic is calculated by finding the difference between two measures of the variable theta and then dividing by the standard deviation of the measurement. For 10 points each:
